title: Adaptive Contrast Token Bridge for Multi-Brand Console
creator: Sofia Ramirez
description:
Problem: Multiple brand themes (Redwood default, partner white-labels, and customer custom palettes) produce inconsistent contrast and elevation meaning in dark mode. Existing theme engine mapping handled basic tokens but breaks for edge cases: nested table zebra stripes, chart color ramps, and button outline states.

Goal: Create an 'Adaptive Contrast Token Bridge' — a small semantic token layer and runtime mapping that sits between brand palettes and component tokens. It should: 1) normalize brand colors into a constrained semantic scale (surface, elevated, text-primary, text-secondary, border, emphasis, interactive), 2) apply contrast-preserving transforms for dark/light inversion, and 3) expose runtime overrides for Dedicated/Private deployments so customers can pin brand variants safely.

Scope: tokens (semantic token set + conversion utilities), component overrides for Button, Table, DataChart, and Badge, small update to CSS variable names used by Console, Figma token libraries, and a visual regression test matrix for brand x theme combinations.
acceptance_criteria: All Console components use semantic tokens and render within WCAG AA for normal-sized text across default and dark themes for Redwood brand and two partner brand palettes.
Buttons (primary/secondary/ghost) maintain focus/hover contrast and visual weight in dark mode without manual per-brand overrides.
Tables: zebra stripes and row hover states maintain row separation in dark themes; borders don't disappear for low-contrast brands.
Charts: color ramps remain distinguishable for up to 8 series, and legend swatches meet contrast thresholds against chart backgrounds.
Runtime manifest allows toggling 'brand-safe mode' for Dedicated/Private with no config changes in app code (feature-flagged).
Automated visual diffs added to CI for three brand palettes x two themes; failure threshold defined in docs.

decisions: Adopt semantic token layer: surface, elevated-1..3, text-primary, text-secondary, border, interactive, emphasis.
Runtime strategy: compute brand->semantic mapping at deployment and ship mappings as JSON manifest to clients for offline mapping. Avoid runtime color math on per-request path.
Prefer CSS variables (prefixed --rwd-) for runtime overrides to minimize component code churn; components read from semantic variables.
Charts: use a contrast-aware color ramp generator with seeded brand accents rather than fixed palettes for each brand.
tradeoffs: Increase token granularity reduces per-component heuristics but adds token maintenance surface area.
Precomputing mappings at deploy reduces runtime CPU but requires more rigorous CI/deployment validation for brand manifests.
Using CSS variables simplifies overrides but means older browsers without var support will need fallback tokens in build step.
risks: Customer brand palettes with near-monochrome colors may still fail contrast thresholds — mitigation: documented escalation path and manual brand review service.
Partner integrations that inject inline styles could bypass CSS variable overrides — mitigation: provide a linter and onboarding checklist for partners.
Visual regression flakiness across environments — mitigation: locked viewport, consistent font stack, and baseline refresh procedure.
qa_checks: Run visual diffs for Redwood + PartnerA + PartnerB palettes across light/dark (automated).
Accessibility audit: run axe-core scans and manual keyboard/contrast checks on Button, Table, Chart pages.
Verify runtime manifest loads for Dedicated/Private deployments and toggles brand-safe mode without reload.
notes: Follow-up: plan a small Design Office Hours with partners to show how brand manifests map into semantic tokens.
Consider adding a 'diagnostics' endpoint in runtime that returns the active token map for support triage.
Longer-term: explore per-component semantic overrides for high-risk components (e.g., heatmaps) in a follow-up cycle.
